title: Dashboard shim layer and metrics lifecycle notes
content:
Context and problem statement:

We have an expanding set of dashboard panels, metric names, and derived signals across runtime, cache, routing, and fallback layers. Over time this has produced:
- duplicate panels with slightly different metric names (avg_latency_ms vs latency_p50_ms)
- ad-hoc renames that break saved queries and onboarding guides
- brittle dashboard wiring when we refactor telemetry or change aggregation semantics

Goals for this proposal:
1) Define a lightweight "shim" layer that sits between raw telemetry producers and dashboards/alerts to provide stable view names, unit conversions, and lifecycle hints.
2) Give a small, actionable lifecycle model (experimental / stable / deprecated / removed) for metrics and dashboard widgets so teams can plan migration.
3) Provide a pragmatic migration checklist and operator-focused dashboard templates for investigation-first workflows (session reconstruction, top-k cause lists, latency heatmaps).

Shim layer: concept and responsibilities
- Purpose: decouple dashboards and saved queries from short-lived telemetry field-level churn. The shim is an index mapping "public signal names" -> one or more raw metrics with transform rules.
- Responsibilities:
  - canonical name registry (human readable identifier + machine id)
  - unit normalization (ms, tokens, counts, bytes)
  - aggregation hint (use p50/p95 count vs raw avg)
  - recommended visualization type hint (time-series, heatmap, table)
  - lifecycle state + owner and last-review date

Implementation notes (minimal viable version):
- YAML/JSON manifest registry stored in repo: observability/shims/registry/*.yaml
- Each manifest entry: id, display_name, raw_series (list), transforms (regex replace, rate(), delta()), unit, recommended_agg, owner, lifecycle, notes, deprecated_since
- Runtime exposure: a small service (or script) that translates dashboard queries at render-time or generates derived PromQL/SQL macros for dashboards.
- Non-blocking: dashboards can reference either shim names (preferred) or raw names. Over time we update dashboards to use shim names.

Metric lifecycle model (four states):
- experimental: newly introduced signal. Short TTL (30–90 days) for validation. Visible in registry with a clear note. No SLA for dashboards that depend on it.
- stable: signal has been validated and accepted for long-term usage. Owner assigned; deprecation requires owners coordination.
- deprecated: marked for removal or rename. Dashboards should be migrated within deprecation window. Deprecated signals still served and available for queries but flagged in UI.
- removed: signal is removed from producers/ingestion. Shim registry keeps a tombstone entry for 12 months for audit.

Migration & rollout plan (for existing panels):
1) Inventory: automatically scan dashboards for raw series names that match any shim registry entries or known raw patterns. Produce an inventory CSV: dashboard, panel id, raw series, suggested shim id.
2) Quick wins: rewrite top 10 high-usage panels to reference shim names (automated PR generator).
3) Owners: for each shim entry mark owner and a migration ETA for dependent dashboards. Report out to owners weekly.
4) Deprecation window: 90 days after an official deprecation note before removing metrics at ingestion. Shorter windows for low-usage signals, longer for infra signals.
5) Removal: on removal, update registry tombstone and create a changelog entry.

Operator-focused widgets (investigation-first templates)
- Session minimal view (vertical): request id, route, model_variant, response_time_ms, kv_cache_hit, fallback_reason, trace_link.
- Latency attribution table: rows grouped by cause bucket (cold-cache, kv-miss, batching-delay, model-queue), columns p50/p95/p99 and count.
- Heatmap: per-route latency vs payload size (buckets), with toggle to overlay token counts.
- Top-k causes panel: for a time window, top 10 keys correlated with high latency (using reverse-index of tags).

Telemetry hygiene checklist (pre-merge for producer teams)
- Add shim registry entry (even experimental) before emitting metric name in prod.
- Include schema: units, cardinality expectations (low/medium/high), max sample rate estimate.
- Add owner and docs short blurb and expected retention.
- If changing aggregation semantics: publish migration note and update affected shim entries.

Example shim registry entry (human readable):
- id: inference.request.latency
  display_name: Inference request latency
  raw_series: ["service.inference.latency_ms", "inference_latency" ]
  transforms: ["coerce_ms", "if name matches '.*_p.*' then keep percentile tag"]
  unit: ms
  recommended_agg: p95
  owner: eng-observability@redwood.example
  lifecycle: stable
  notes: "Canonical latency metric for inference path, normalized to ms. Prefer p95 for SLOs."

Open questions / risks
- Ownership overhead: who maintains the registry? Suggest rotating stewards per quarter (eng-observability + serving-runtime liaison).
- Query performance: translating shim names to complex PromQL might affect dashboard latency; need to cache generated queries.
- Adoption: engineering teams need low-friction migration (automated PRs and clear templates).
- Backwards compatibility: must keep tombstones and mapping for at least 12 months, otherwise saved looks break.

Immediate next steps (2-week sprint):
- Prototype registry format and check-in to repo (owner: Ava)
- Small generator script to scan dashboards and output suggested rewrites (owner: Liam)
- Create three operator investigation templates and a sample dashboard using shim names (owner: Priya)
- Draft internal announcement and migration guidelines (owner: Mateo)

Notes-to-self:
- Keep the initial registry narrow: focus on top 30 signals used in incident runbooks.
- Add a "confidence" field for each mapping to mark how reliable a raw_series -> shim mapping is.

Related artifacts and references:
- Migration checklist draft: CONFLUENCE-OBS-1824
- Dashboard templates repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/observability/tree/main/templates

End of notes.
